title: Approaching I/O-optimality for Approximate Attention
claim: A large matrix product is computed by tiling the output and accumulating partial products from matching row and column strips of the inputs.
layout: 3 matrices in L-shape, arrows from input tiles to output tile, dimension brackets
description: A grayscale schematic of tiled matrix multiplication. The lower-left matrix U1 has dimensions n×r. The upper-right matrix H has dimensions r×d. The lower-right output matrix is n×d. Gray brackets along the edges label the dimensions n, r, d and r. Each matrix has a thick gray rectangle in its top-left corner marking a tile. The tile in U1 has width t3. The output tile is t1 tall and t2 wide. A thick gray arrow runs from the U1 tile to the output tile. Another thick gray arrow runs down from the H tile to the output tile. Thin black arrows point from the matrices toward the output to show the sweep across the full row and column strips. The eye goes first to the thick tiles and the arrows pointing at the output tile. The figure has no color and no text beyond the math symbols.
caption: Illustration of matrix multiplication with tiles, for the example $\matU_1 \matH$. The output matrix is split to tiles of size $t_1 \times t_2$, and each of these is aggregated in tiles of width $t_3$ (respectively, height $t_3$) in the corresponding row strip of $\matU_1$ (column strip of $\matH$). Altogether, the output matrix is computed via $\frac{n}{t_1} \cdot \frac{d}{t_2} \cdot \frac{r}{t_3}$ tiling steps.
abstract: We revisit the I/O complexity of attention in large language models. Given query-key-value matrices $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, and a machine with fast memory size $M$, the goal is to compute the "attention matrix" $A=\text{softmax}(Q K ^{\top}/\sqrt{d}) V$ with the minimal number of data transfers between fast and slow memory. Existing methods in the literature, most notably FlashAttention and its variants, incur an I/O cost that depends quadratically on the context length $n$, while a trivial lower bound only requires $Î©(nd)$ I/O's to read the inputs and write the output. In this work we show that the dependence on $n$ can be reduced to almost-linear, by developing I/O-efficient algorithms inspired by the recent approximate attention method of Alman and Song [NeurIPS'23]. We also provide (algorithm-specific) lower bounds in different parameter regimes, which nearly match the corresponding upper bounds, indicating that the proposed algorithms are indeed close to I/O-optimal.
